## Introduction

In these exercises, you'll practice with Unix commands,
especially those that operate on files as seen in this week's classes.

_In general, you should use Unix commands for all exercises._
_E.g., if you are asked to check a file size, don't do so in the OnDemand file browser!_

### Setting up

- Start a VS Code session through OSC OnDemand in the folder
  `/fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER`.
- Create and use a Markdown file to keep notes on what you're doing.
- You'll use the @garrigós2025 data files,
  which you should have stored as `garrigos-data` in the above dir.

<details><summary>_Click here for instructions if you need to (re)download these files_</summary>
```bash
# Make sure you're in your personal dir:
cd /fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER
  
git clone https://github.com/jelmerp/garrigos-data
```
</details>

## Exercise 1: Miscellaneous

_Your starting point working dir should be `/fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER`_

1. Create a dir `week03/ex1` within `/fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER`, and navigate there.
   _Use this as the working dir for all following questions in this exercise,_
   _so avoid navigating anywhere else._
   
1. What is the size of the `metadata.tsv` file of the @garrigós2025 data set?

2. Copy the `ref` dir of the @garrigós2025 data set to your current working dir,

3. Run the following command:


   keeping the same file name.

5. Do you think you will now be able to succesfully run `rmdir ref_copy`?
   Try it.

## Exercise 2: Moving, copying and removing dummy FASTQ files

1. Create a dir `week03/ex2` within `/fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER`, and navigate there.
   _Use this as the working dir for all following questions in this exercise,_
   _so avoid navigating anywhere else._

2. Create a new dir `seqs`,
   and use the below command to create some dummy FASTQ files in there.
   Then, check the result with `ls` and use a command to get a count of the number
   of files you created.

   ```bash
   # [This command uses a trick called 'brace expansion' to create many files at once.]
   # [You don't need to understand how this works.]
   touch seqs/sample{01..25}_R{1,2}.fastq
   ```

3. Copy the dummy FASTA files for samples `01` through `09` into your working dir
   with a single command.

4. Remove the files you just copied and when doing so,
   make the command report what it's doing.

5. Move all R1 files into a dir `seqs_R1`, and then rename `seqs`,
   which should now only contain R2 files, to `seqs_R1`.

6. Copy the Garrigos et al. metadata file into your current working dir,
   giving the copy the name `garrigos_metadata.tsv`.

## Exercise 3: Nuances of `cp` and `mv` behavior

For both `cp` and `mv`, when operating on files
(and this works equivalently for directories):

- If the destination path is an existing dir,
  the file will go into that dir and keep its original name.
- If the destination path is _not_ an existing dir,
  the (last bit of the) destination specifies the new file name.
- A trailing slash in the destination path makes explicit that you are referring
  to a dir and not a file.

With that in mind, try to answer these questions about the following command:

```bash
cp newfile2.txt more_data/
```

1. What do you think the command would do or attempt to do?
2. Do you think the command will succeed (given what is in your `sandbox` dir)?
3. What would the command have done if you had omitted the trailing forward slash?

## Solutions

### Exercise 1

<details><summary>**1.** Create a new dir and navigate there</summary>

This assumes you start in `/fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER`:

```bash
mkdir week03/ex1
cd week03/ex1
```

(You could also `cd week03` first, and then create the dir and navigate there.)

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** What is the size of the `metadata.tsv` file?</summary>

It is 633 bytes:

```bash
ls -lh ../../garrigos-data/meta/metadata.tsv
```
```bash-out
-rw-rw----+ 1 jelmer PAS0471 633 Sep  7 09:05 metadata.tsv
```
</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Copy the `ref` dir to `ref_copy`</summary>

Because you are copying a dir, you will need the `-r` (recursive) option:

```bash
cp -r ../../garrigos-data/ref ref_copy
```
</details>

<details><summary>**4.** Run the `rmdir` command</summary>

```bash
rmdir ref_copy
```
```bash-out
rmdir: failed to remove 'ref_copy': Directory not empty
```

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** Move the GTF file in `ref_copy` to your current working dir</summary>

To keep the same filename,
remember to simply use the `.` shortcut for the current working dir as the destination:

```bash
mv ref_copy/GCF_016801865.2.gtf.gz .
```

</details>

<details><summary>**6.** Do you think you will now be able to succesfully run `rmdir ref_copy`?</summary>

Yes, because the `ref_copy` dir is now empty, this will work:

```bash
# [No output means it succeeds!]
rmdir ref_copy
```

Let's check:

```bash
ls
```
```bash-out
GCF_016801865.2.gtf.gz
```

</details>

### Exercise 2

<details><summary>**1.** Create a new dir and navigate there</summary>

Assuming you're doing this right after exercise 1,
you should be in `/fs/ess/PAS2880/users/$USER/week03/ex1`,
in which case the following commands work:

```bash
mkdir ../ex2
cd ../ex2
```
</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Create a dir with dummy sequence files</summary>

- Create the dir:

  ```bash
  mkdir seqs
  ```

- Create the dummy files:

  ```bash
  touch seqs/sample{01..25}_R{1,2}.fastq
  ```
  
  This uses a construct called **brace expansion**, which we won't cover in class.

- Check the result:

  ```bash
  ls seqs
  ```
  ```bash-out
  sample01_R1.fastq  sample03_R1.fastq  sample05_R1.fastq  sample07_R1.fastq  sample09_R1.fastq  sample11_R1.fastq  sample13_R1.fastq  sample15_R1.fastq  sample17_R1.fastq  sample19_R1.fastq  sample21_R1.fastq  sample23_R1.fastq  sample25_R1.fastq
sample01_R2.fastq  sample03_R2.fastq  sample05_R2.fastq  sample07_R2.fastq  sample09_R2.fastq  sample11_R2.fastq  sample13_R2.fastq  sample15_R2.fastq  sample17_R2.fastq  sample19_R2.fastq  sample21_R2.fastq  sample23_R2.fastq  sample25_R2.fastq
sample02_R1.fastq  sample04_R1.fastq  sample06_R1.fastq  sample08_R1.fastq  sample10_R1.fastq  sample12_R1.fastq  sample14_R1.fastq  sample16_R1.fastq  sample18_R1.fastq  sample20_R1.fastq  sample22_R1.fastq  sample24_R1.fastq
sample02_R2.fastq  sample04_R2.fastq  sample06_R2.fastq  sample08_R2.fastq  sample10_R2.fastq  sample12_R2.fastq  sample14_R2.fastq  sample16_R2.fastq  sample18_R2.fastq  sample20_R2.fastq  sample22_R2.fastq  sample24_R2.fastq
  ```

- Count the number of files:

  ```bash
  ls seqs | wc -l
  ```
  ```bash-out
  50
  ```

  Note that this gives the correct count even though when printed to screen,
  `ls` output typically used multiple columns and therefore shows more than one
  file per line.
  
  In contrast,
  the count from `ls -l` is _not_ correct, since its output includes a header line:
  
  ```bash
  ls -l seqs | wc -l
  ```
  ```bash-out
  51
  ```

</details>

### Exercise 3

<details><summary>**1.** What do you think the command would do or attempt to do?</summary>

Because we added a trailing forward slash to `more_data/`,
we are making clear that we are referring to a directory.
So the command will attempt to copy the file into a dir `more_data`,
with the file keeping the same name.

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Do you think the command will succeed?</summary>

The `more_data/` dir does not exist,
and `cp` will not create a dir on the fly -- so it will fail:

```bash
cp newfile2.txt more_data/
```
```bash-out
cp: cannot create regular file ‘more_data/’: Not a directory
```
</details>

<details><summary>**3.** What would the command have done if you had omitted the trailing forward slash?</summary>

If you had omitted the trailing forward slash,
it would have created a copy of the file with *file* name `more_data`
(if that seems confusing: note that in Unix, files don't need to have a file
extension).

P.S.: To copy the file according to the original intention,
first create the destination dir and then copy:

```bash
mkdir more_data
cp newfile2.txt more_data/
```
  
Note also that once the `more_data` dir exists,
it **does not** make a difference whether or not you using a trailing slash.

</details>
